title: Blackwater
text:
Blackwater Receiving smelled like machine oil and ozone, and under that the cold that settles inside big structures where the air never moves. The access gate took <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s spoofed credentials without complaint. It logged them under a maintenance sub-contractor — a defunct hydraulics outfit that had left its licensing just loose enough to borrow.

"The company isn't real," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, walking the B-platform.

"The company was real for four years and paid its insurance on time," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "The ID is a monument. Stop worrying about it."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> had told him on the ride over — flat, the way she said anything that cost her something: her brother worked receiving here, and her brother was the whole reason this favor existed instead of a straight contract. "His name's <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5fec-71c8-8373-06bc52e70b70">Kofi</entity>," she'd said. "Don't make me regret the introduction."

The yard's freight slugs waited in the staging bays — matte gray shells the length of a transit car, rated to Mach 6 in the vacuum tube, parked now on pneumatic dollies. They were huge. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took them in and kept walking.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5fec-71c8-8373-06bc52e70b70">Kofi Mensah</entity> was on A-platform, running manifest checks with two other loaders. He was thicker than his sister but moved the same spare way she did. He had not been sleeping. It showed — the look of a man watched by a clock he hadn't set.

He saw <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> and <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> together at the platform end and stopped moving for a second or two.

"You called it," he said to his sister, when they were close enough.

"I called it," she said.

"You called it on a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>."

"I called it on THE <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>." She said it like a line she'd been deciding how to say since the freight lift that morning. "His rate is fine. It's a favor."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5fec-71c8-8373-06bc52e70b70">Kofi</entity> looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> straight — a man with a habit of spending carefully. "Parr knows something's coming," he said. "He's been doing the reconciliations himself. Terminal three, Gate 3, every day between 13:00 and 14:00. Alone. That's where the gap is — I can see in my own manifest that units got re-logged under a different container class after the batch was sealed. I can't touch the terminal. I'm flagged as a subject of inquiry."

"I can," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I need thirteen minutes at Gate 3."

"The gap window is eleven minutes."

"I know." He said it the way he priced a job — flat, closed, no room in it for the two minutes he didn't have. It came out harder than the sentence needed, and he heard it land that way.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5fec-71c8-8373-06bc52e70b70">Kofi</entity> thought about it. "B-platform's outbound is ninety seconds late every shift."

"I know that too." Same register. Same lack of give. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity>'s eyes moved off her brother and onto <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> for a beat longer than the exchange required — reading it, the way she'd read the box truck, the way she'd read a five-year license and priced a stranger's gear off a rotation deal. Whatever she found, she didn't say.

The clearance panel above A-platform went green. Somewhere below the floor the first inbound slug slowed out of transit speed with a sound like a building drawing breath.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went in at 13:11, inside the gap, while the inbound clearance light still cycled red and the B-platform corridor ran its ninety-second lag. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was outside with the schematic on her terminal and both countdown panels in view.

The reconciliation files were built for deniability. Problem entries reclassified under a container category that legitimately handled mixed cargo. Timestamps that read like clerical error to anyone who didn't know better.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew better.

He found the re-logs for the Φ12,000 microprinter batch. Original manifest clean, sealed under Kofi's ID at 21:43 six days back. The reclassification entered at 02:17 the next morning, under a supervisor override that resolved to Parr.

Outside the window, the outbound clearance panel clicked from amber to red. Six minutes.

He copied the records, the timestamps, and the override ID into a sealed package flagged for yard security. Then he entered Parr's override code as the revised source of record in the formal inquiry. The system accepted it. It was accurate. Kofi's name had been on the filing four days too long.

ADDENDUM TO INQUIRY 7741-R: REVISED SOURCE OF RECORD. SUPERVISOR OVERRIDE 09-PAR, TIMESTAMP 02:17. SEE ATTACHED RECONCILIATION DIFF.

He hit submit at 13:18.

"Three minutes," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said on comms.

He was out of Gate 3 at 13:19.

The records were corrected, on the record, under Parr's own credentials. What it would cost him, he'd find out later.

But the system flagged the amendment before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> reached the platform exit.

The terminal chimed — a soft, procedural sound, nothing urgent. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> kept walking. The chime repeated. Then a third time, and this one carried a different harmonic, the way a machine sounds when it's asking instead of telling. His neuretics picked up the resonance: 17.3 Hz, the same base frequency as the carousel junction.

He stopped.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s voice came through the comms, tight. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. The amendment just pinged back as *unverifiable*."

"What does that mean."

"It means the system is asking for secondary validation. Parr's override code is flagged as *dormant* — he hasn't used it in seventeen days. The system is requesting manual approval from the next authority level up."

Six minutes. The B-platform outbound was now on borrowed time.

"Can you kill it."

"No. I can't touch yard systems from outside. And if I try to access remotely, it logs as an intrusion attempt." A half-second pause. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, the harmonic just shifted. 17.415 Hz. That's — "

"I know what it is."

The terminal chimed again. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned back toward Gate 3. The corridor behind him was empty. The inbound slug was somewhere below, slowing down the way Kofi had said — like a building drawing breath.

He went back in.

The terminal screen displayed a single line: AWAITING MANUAL VERIFICATION. SUPERVISOR AUTHORITY REQUIRED. REQUEST TIMEOUT: 4:47.

Parr wasn't in the office. The chair was empty, the terminal dark, the window onto the staging bay showing nothing but the freight slugs waiting in their bays like patient animals.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the screen a second time. The harmonic shifted again — 17.771 Hz — and his implant logged it without asking, the way it had logged everything else for eleven years. Everything that looked like coincidence. Everything that looked like a system breaking exactly the way it needed to break.

*There is no inside.*

The words surfaced without source. Not from <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>. Not from the entity. Just there, the way understanding sometimes arrives as a full sentence instead of a process.

He pulled Parr's override code from the system log — the one that had just been flagged as dormant. Then he entered it again, this time not as the source of the variance but as the witness to it, in the *supervisor authorization* field instead of the amendment field. Not as the man who made the decision. As the man who was made to make it. The system hesitated for 0.8 seconds — churned, considered — then it accepted it.

MANUAL VERIFICATION COMPLETE. SOURCE: SUPERVISOR OVERRIDE 09-PAR. AMENDMENT APPROVED.

The terminal chimed once and went dark.

Outside, the outbound clearance panel switched from red to green.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked out at 13:24. Over the window. The B-platform was already moving — the slug pulling out on its pneumatic dolly with <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s spoofed credentials logged as the last maintenance check, the one that cleared it for transit. It rolled slow at first, then faster, the loading mechanism engaging as it approached the induction gate, and it cleared the launch gate with a sound like a door closing on something that had been holding its breath.

Kofi was still on A-platform, watching the outbound go. He saw <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> exit Gate 3 and nodded once, the smallest movement, the way a man nods when a debt gets paid and nobody needs to say it out loud — the kind a man makes when a clock he didn't set finally stops.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was waiting at the access gate, field kit already packed. "The system is going to realize Parr's override code was used twice in seven minutes," she said. "It's going to start asking questions about why a dormant code just came alive."

"It's going to ask Parr," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"And Parr is going to have to explain how he was in two places at once, or admit someone spoofed his credentials, or claim the terminal malfunctioned. Any of those answers costs him."

"Yes."

They walked the B-platform back toward the exit. Behind them, the inbound slug was already docking, the pneumatic hiss of the coupling loud enough to cover the sound of the terminal chiming one more time — 17.3 Hz again, a harmonic asking a question it already knew the answer to.

"The entity did this," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. It wasn't a question.

"No." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pushed through the access gate. "The system did this. I just asked it the right question."

But the harmonic followed him out into the machine oil and ozone, and he knew — the way he'd known about the carousel, the way he'd known about the eleven years — that asking and being answered were not the same thing as choosing.

The entity was still routing him.

It had just learned to do it without saying a word.

Parr was not a big man. He carried twelve years of institutional weight and moved like it — steady, unhurried. Once that unhurried had been confidence. Lately it had turned to care. He came onto the B-platform at 13:31 with a terminal in his hand and the face of a man whose reconciliation filing had just pinged him about a revision.

He saw <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> first, because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was standing in the open, positioned so the sight lines ran through the corridor instead of the office. Then he saw Kofi on the platform behind him. Then he looked at the terminal again.

"You're not yard security," he said.

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"You filed under my code."

"Your code filed under your code. I just found where it had been." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> held up his own terminal and turned the display so Parr could read it from where he stood. The original manifest, clean, Kofi's signature at 21:43. Then the reclassification, 02:17 the next morning, supervisor override 09-PAR resolving back to his own ID like a mirror he couldn't look away from. "The re-log was at 02:17. Your override pulled the microprinter batch out of Kofi's manifest and reclassified it under mixed cargo — the category that doesn't carry the same audit trail. The original manifest was clean. The inquiry's been revised to show the actual source."

Parr's jaw tightened. He read it twice. His code had been sitting dormant, flagged, waiting for someone to explain why it had come alive at two in the morning. Now that someone was going to be him.

He was quiet long enough for the panel overhead to blink once. He'd run a bad play. He'd known it was bad and run it anyway. Now it had caught up with him.

"How much do they have you for?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Fourteen thousand. Rate adjusts." He looked at Kofi. "I needed one clean lift. Filed it back the whole way. Reclassified the batch under a container code so nobody would notice. One small override. Nobody was supposed to—" He stopped. "He was the easiest manifest to fit?"

"He was. You'll want to talk to yard security."

"I know." The relief of a man who'd been bracing for the landing. "The collectors. They'll—"

"That's a separate problem," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Start with security."

The two men came off the south platform access at 13:47, while the second inbound slug was still slowing in the bay. They had the look of men on a fee — loose, unhurried, taking their time over ground they'd already walked. Not tall, but dense, the kind of frame that comes from carrying other people's problems for a living. They'd seen <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> come out of Gate 3 and worked out what it meant.

One carried a shock-bar clipped to his belt. The other had his hands free, which in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s experience was worse. Down his left forearm a strip of chromatophore panel cycled a debt-collection license in three languages, the way street collectors wore their paper where a hand couldn't reach it and a court could always read it.

"Yard's private property," the first said. "You're not credentialed?"

"I was," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Hydraulics maintenance, sub-contract, third-party audit. I signed out at the gate." He watched both of them, and the slug bay behind them, and the panel overhead. Amber. Two minutes to outbound clearance. "You should go."

"The man we're here about," the second said, nodding back toward where Parr had gone, "has a payment arrangement. Fourteen thousand QUANTA plus adjudication fees, and the window closed at noon. Arrangements don't get renegotiated by freelancers."

"The arrangement already changed," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Yard security has his statement."

They looked at each other. The first one unclipped the shock-bar.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand did not move toward <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>. It wanted to. The want was old, load-bearing, a decade of jobs where the shotgun ended the conversation before the conversation cost him anything — and he set the want aside the way he'd set aside a hundred smaller ones, without deciding to, the way you don't decide to keep your hand off a stove twice.

The shock-bar came in high and right — the obvious side. The second man went low and left, reading off the first move. A pincer. It would have worked on a man who needed room to draw. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wasn't drawing. He stepped inside the swing before it was halfway out, caught the man's wrist in both hands, and turned the bar's own momentum up and over the man's shoulder. The shock-bar fired against its owner's jacket. He sat down hard on the platform, blinking, deeply surprised.

The second man had reach and used it. A solid shove put <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> back two steps to the platform edge. Ribs pulled where a rib had gone bad two jobs ago; the eat-the-wince reflex fired before the pain finished registering. Two steps back was two steps toward the slug bay. The outbound panel had gone green. The floor hummed — the 13:47 building to transit speed in the tube below.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> used one of those steps. He turned the man's next move aside, planted a heel on the edge for leverage, and brought his forearm across the collarbone. Not hard enough to break anything. Hard enough to end it. The second man sat down beside the first. Behind them the freight pod tore away down the tube, several tons of it, roaring.

Both men on the ground. Both breathing. Neither one bleeding from a blade he hadn't drawn, which was the entire point of not drawing it, and which cost him nothing anyone standing here could see. Geometry and timing and the discipline of understanding that most violence is just people moving through space in predictable ways.

"The 13:47 is on time today," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

Neither of them said anything. The one with the license panel breathed hard through his nose, the way a man breathes when he's working out how this had gone wrong so fast, and whether the debt was worth whatever came next.

He left them on the platform and went to find <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>. The ribs told him about it with every step, a small honest bill come due, and he let them.

The operations supervisor was a woman named Dreis. She'd been handed a great deal of information in the last twenty minutes and was working through it with the flat annoyance of someone whose day had become somebody else's problem. She shook <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand at 15:00 and gave him a receipt.

The receipt read, formally:

BLACKWATER RECEIVING — INQUIRY CLOSURE 7741-R.
SUBJECT: MENSAH, K. CHARGE: VACATED PER REVISED SOURCE OF RECORD.
DEBT-COURT FILING: RETRACTED.
SUPERVISOR PARR B. STATUS: SUSPENDED, PENDING REVIEW. RESTITUTION HEARING SCHEDULED.
NOTE: YARD SECURITY EXTENDS APPRECIATION FOR THIRD-PARTY AUDIT ASSISTANCE.
NOTE: YARD MANAGEMENT WOULD LIKE TO DISCUSS A STANDING AUDIT ARRANGEMENT.
NOTE: PENDING ARRANGEMENTS WITH YARD MANAGEMENT = OWED ONE (1) QUIET FAVOR, SCOPE: TBD, RATE: STANDARD.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the last line.

"Standard terms," he said, which was either agreement or reflex. Dreis nodded — brisk, a woman who had added a line to a budget and closed the window on it. "You come in, you look at what we ask you to look at, you tell us what's broken," she said, already turning her terminal back to face herself. "You find something like Parr, we handle it in-house. You find something bigger, you stop looking and you call us."

Which was the whole offer, laid flat. They wanted a canary. Someone who could move through their systems without tripping the alerts that brought in the corporate auditors — the ones who didn't stop at suspension, who went straight to dismantling. Early warning, at standard rate, in exchange for the leash that came stapled to it.

Outside, on A-platform, <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> had a hand on her brother's arm and wasn't talking. Kofi was looking at the receipt on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s terminal the way a man reads something that changes a number.

"Cleared," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "On the record."

Kofi took a long breath. Pressed his thumbnail to the corner of the receipt, the way you press to keep a thing from disappearing if you stop holding it.

"What do I owe you?" he asked.

"You don't," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Your sister did."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> looked at him. Her panels cycled from pharma-blue down to a low off-white — a rest state, or a power-save. "I want to run transport on your contract," she said, quietly. "When you need a driver, a loader, someone who knows the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> yard schedules." She said it like the favor was being paid back in installments she'd already worked out. "Permanent arrangement. My rate is fair."

"I know your rate," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I looked you up."

"And?"

"Reasonable," he said. It wasn't effusive, and he meant it exactly that way, and she took it exactly that way.

"You didn't have to ask," he added. "You had to make the offer. There's a difference."

"Is there."

"One of them's a favor. The other one's a job."

Something moved at the corner of her mouth, small, and settled. They didn't shake hands. The terms were already set.

Kofi was clear. Parr was accountable. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had a transport ally on a standing arrangement. Against that: the yard now knew when he was available, and the chain around him had one more link than it had that morning.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> and <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> had never left the holster.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> made it to the break room before the terminal chimed.

The room smelled like burnt coffee and the particular staleness of a space that had never seen daylight. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was at the small table with three empty cups and a logistics schematic hanging over the table in her overlay—the yard's outbound manifest system, which she'd accessed the way she accessed everything, which was to say completely and without asking.

She looked up when he came in. Took in the platform dust on his jacket, the way he was moving, the absence of visible blood.

"Two guys," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Parr's money. Didn't land."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> nodded. Didn't ask if he'd hurt them, which meant she already knew he had—just not badly. She folded the projection away.

"We've got a problem," she said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat. The ribs let him know about it.

"The receipt you got," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> continued. She threw the schematic back up between them, then pulled up an image. A document scan—the formal retraction from Blackwater's systems. "I grabbed the metadata before Dreis closed the window. File was created at 09:47:03 this morning."

"When they terminated the D-class."

"When they terminated the *order* to terminate the D-class," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. She zoomed in on a field <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wouldn't have known to read. "This isn't a correction. This is an override. Someone with system access revoked Parr's original suspension and filed a counter-retraction in the same minute the infrastructure authority was supposed to execute the decommission."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited.

"Someone with access to both the yard's administrative systems and the regional authority's work-order database. On the same clock. Same timestamp down to the second."

The terminal chimed again. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s personal unit, sitting on the table between them. He didn't reach for it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> did. She read the new posting.

"Oh," she said quietly.

She turned the screen toward him.

STANDING CONTRACT — ACKNOWLEDGMENT.
CLIENT HAS REVIEWED TODAY'S FILING (INQUIRY 7741-R, BLACKWATER RECEIVING).
CLIENT NOTES: DEBT-COURT DOCKET CLOSED. RECORD CLEAR.
CLIENT NOTES: THE 13:47 WAS ON TIME.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT HAS AUDITED BLACKWATER'S COLLECTOR ACCOUNTS FOR PARR, B.
ADDENDUM: THE COLLECTION AGENCY HOLDING PARR'S DEBT IS A REGISTERED SHELL.
ADDENDUM: THE SHELL'S PARENT ENTITY IS A SHELL.
ADDENDUM: THE PARENT'S PARENT IS A SHELL.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT RECOGNIZES THE FLAVOR.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT ADVISES: SABLE SHOULD SEE THIS.
NOTE: RIA MENSAH'S PULSE YARD SCHEDULING DATA HAS BEEN ADDED TO STANDING CONTRACT SCOPE AS A SUPPLEMENTARY RESOURCE. WITH HER PERMISSION. CLIENT ASKED.
NOTE: SHE SAID YES.
NOTE: IOWA CORRIDOR TRANSIT WINDOWS NOTED FOR RECORD. CLIENT HAS FILED FOR FUTURE REFERENCE.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it twice. The break room suddenly felt very small.
